body: {"total":8,"records":[{"title":"Silver diamine fluoride in school-based dental programmes: caries arrest at six and twelve months","authors":"Oyelaran-Stroud M, Bergstrom-Achebe T, Rao-Whitfield K","year":2020,"venue":"Ashcombe Community Dental Health","doi":"10.5555/acdh.2020.0158","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We followed 1,122 children aged 5 to 11 who received silver diamine fluoride for active cavities in a school-based programme. Six months after one application, 72 percent of treated lesions were arrested; among lesions that received a second application at six months, 81 percent were arrested at twelve months. Arrest was lower on lesions that were large and on teeth that were hard to dry in the portable chair. No serious adverse events were recorded. Parents of 6 percent of treated children complained about staining. Children lost to follow-up were more often from schools in deprived areas, so arrest rates may be optimistic."},{"title":"Parental acceptability of staining after silver diamine fluoride: choices and conversations","authors":"Lindqvist-Ayodele R, Moreau-Chen P","year":2021,"venue":"Vellmar Paediatric Dentistry Reports","doi":"10.5555/vpdr.2021.0092","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We asked 412 parents of children in school dental programmes to choose between treatment options shown with photographs, and held conversations with 30 of them. Staining after silver diamine fluoride was acceptable to 67 percent of parents on back teeth and to 29 percent on front teeth. Acceptance rose when the alternative was a general anaesthetic or a long wait, and when the photograph showed the stain on a back tooth. Parents wanted to see a photograph before agreeing and resented hearing about the stain only afterwards. Parents who took part in conversations were more often fluent in the majority language than the whole sample."},{"title":"Consent return as the bottleneck in school dental programmes: a process mapping study","authors":"Achterberg-Nkosi F, Duarte-Holm J","year":2019,"venue":"Harthill Oral Health Services Letters","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We mapped the steps from dental screening to treatment in four school dental programmes and timed each step for 600 children. The median time to consent return was 16 days, and 22 percent of consent forms were never returned. Waiting for consent accounted for most of the time between screening and treatment, while chair time was a small share. Forms were lost between school bags, class teachers and the school office. Programmes that sent forms home with a reminder text to parents had faster return. The study did not record the language spoken at home, so it could not say who was least likely to return a form."},{"title":"Lean redesign of a school dental clinic day: value stream mapping and chair utilisation","authors":"Petrakis-Oduya S, Hallberg-Mensah D, Ferreira-Lau N","year":2023,"venue":"Greyhaven Improvement Letters","doi":"10.5555/gil.2023.0204","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"A school dental team used value stream mapping to redesign its clinic day across eight schools. Changes included a call-from-class list ordered by treatment need, preparation of instruments before children arrived and a single consent check at the door. Chair utilisation rose from 48 percent to 71 percent over two terms, and the number of children treated per clinic day rose from 11 to 16. Therapists reported less time spent waiting for children to be found in class. The evaluation used before-after data without a comparison group, and a new appointment clerk started during the second term."},{"title":"Language, consent and treatment in school dental programmes: who is left out?","authors":"Kimani-Osei L, Varga-Tanaka B","year":2024,"venue":"Ashcombe Community Dental Health","doi":"10.5555/acdh.2024.0071","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Using records from a school dental programme serving 31 schools, we linked the language spoken at home to consent return and treatment. Children from families with limited proficiency in the majority language were less likely to have a consent form returned (adjusted odds ratio 0.43) and waited longer for treatment when a form was returned. Translated forms alone made little difference, while a phone call from a bilingual staff member increased return. Children with untreated cavities at the end of the year were concentrated in these families. Home language was missing for 14 percent of children, which may bias the estimates."},{"title":"Application time and child cooperation for silver diamine fluoride in mobile school clinics","authors":"Brennan-Iwu C, Sato-Lindgren E","year":2016,"venue":"Vellmar Paediatric Dentistry Reports","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We timed silver diamine fluoride applications for 214 children in mobile school clinics and recorded cooperation on a simple scale. The median chair time for application was 4 minutes, compared with 22 minutes for a small restoration in the same clinics. Younger children and children who had not visited a dentist before were less cooperative, but most applications were completed at the first attempt. Time spent finding children in class and waiting for them to arrive exceeded chair time on most clinic days. The study was conducted by two experienced therapists, which may limit how far the timings apply to other teams."},{"title":"Combined versus separate consent forms for preventive and non-invasive dental treatment in schools","authors":"Mahlangu-Frost D, Quist-Ibarra A","year":2022,"venue":"Harthill Oral Health Services Letters","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Twelve schools in one programme replaced separate consent forms for examination, fluoride varnish and silver diamine fluoride with a single combined form, while twelve other schools kept separate forms. The combined consent form raised consent return from 58 to 74 percent, while return in schools with separate forms was unchanged. The proportion of parents who ticked the box refusing silver diamine fluoride on the combined form was 11 percent. Schools were not allocated at random, and the combined form included a photograph of staining, so the effects of the two changes cannot be separated."},{"title":"Teachers' views of dental clinics in primary schools: disruption, support and responsibility","authors":"Olawale-Hartmann S, Castellanos-Mbeki R","year":2025,"venue":"Greyhaven Improvement Letters","doi":"10.5555/gil.2025.0019","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We held structured conversations with 26 teachers and 9 school office staff in schools that host a dental clinic. Teachers supported the clinics but described disruption when children were called from lessons at unpredictable times, and some said they were left to explain treatment to anxious parents. Office staff were often responsible for chasing consent forms without being told why forms mattered. Participants suggested a timetable agreed in advance and a single point of contact in the dental team. Teachers were recruited through head teachers who favoured the programme, which may have limited critical views."}]}
